hazards.blow-the-dust-away: You went to blow the dust off the card. Blowing lifts the finest dust into the air, where people breathe it. Builders use a special vacuum to pick dust up instead, and the class does the same with the little vacuum.
hazards.dust-is-just-dirt: You said concrete dust is just dirt. Concrete has sand and stone in it, and drilling grinds some of that into dust finer than you can see. That fine dust is why builders catch it at the drill instead of letting it float around.
hazards.sweep-the-floor-dry: You picked up a dry brush to sweep the bench. A dry brush throws fine dust back into the air. Builders use a vacuum or a damp cloth, so the dust ends up in the bag and not in anyone's breath.
hazards.walk-under-the-drill: You started toward the crew's real drill. The crew is working, and visitors watch from behind the rope with the crew lead. Everything the class needs to see is on the model bench.

interrupts.alert: The little vacuum hose slips off the model drill's shroud and a puff of dust appears.
interrupts.cue: Stop the model drill first, then fix the hose.
interrupts.missNote: The model drill kept running while the hose hung loose, and a little cloud settled on the bench.
interrupts.why: When the hose comes off, the shroud stops catching dust. Stopping the drill stops the dust right away, and then the hose goes back on. The real crew does exactly the same when their hose slips.
interrupts.wrongNote: That leaves the drill running. Stop the drill first. Choose the response that deals with it now.

interrupts.alert: Dust from another crew's work drifts toward the class on the breeze.
interrupts.cue: Step aside out of the dust's path with the crew lead, who asks the other crew to stop.
interrupts.missNote: The class stayed in the dust's path until the crew lead moved everyone aside, upwind of the drill.
interrupts.why: Dust from someone else's tool is still dust to breathe. Stepping out of its path is the quick fix, and asking the other crew to catch their dust fixes the cause. Speaking up about dust is part of working safely together.
interrupts.wrongNote: That stays in the dust's path. Step aside first. Choose the response that deals with it now.

lateNotes.sld-checkin: The check-in comes at the very end of the visit.
lateNotes.sld-plan-log: The dust plan record is written after both drill runs — nothing to record yet.

name: Dust You Cannot See at a Building Site

passRule.note: stars >= 2 and no unsafe action (WebXR/shared/records.js passed())

steps.cue: Mark the three things the crew uses to keep drilling dust out of the air.

decoyNotes.sld-radio: Useful for talking, but it catches no dust.

itemNames.sld-shroud: the shroud around the drill bit
itemNames.sld-water: the water line on the core drill

itemNotes.sld-hepa: Its filter keeps the finest dust inside.
itemNotes.sld-shroud: It pulls dust into the vacuum hose.
itemNotes.sld-water: It turns the dust into wet mud.

steps.prompt: Mark the three things the crew uses to keep drilling dust out of the air.
steps.title: Find the tools that catch the dust
steps.why: A crew drilling concrete has more than one way to catch dust. A shroud around the drill bit pulls dust into a vacuum hose, a water line keeps a bigger drill wet so the dust turns to mud, and a special vacuum cleans the holes afterwards. Each one stops dust before it reaches the air people breathe.

steps.cue: Lay a clean dark card, drill the model without the shroud, look at the card, then a fresh card and drill with the shroud on.

itemNames.sld-ord-bare: 2 · drill the model block without the shroud
itemNames.sld-ord-card: 1 · lay a clean dark card beside the block
itemNames.sld-ord-look: 3 · look at the dust on the card
itemNames.sld-ord-shroud: 4 · lay a fresh card and drill with the shroud on

steps.outOfOrderNote: Out of order. Start with a clean dark card beside the model block.
steps.prompt: Lay a clean dark card, drill the model without the shroud, look at the card, then a fresh card and drill with the shroud on.
steps.title: Put the dust test in order
steps.why: A fair test changes only one thing. A clean dark card each time shows exactly how much dust landed. Drilling once without the shroud and once with it, on the same model block for the same time, shows what the shroud catches, because the shroud is the only change. Without the clean card, old dust would mix into the new reading.

steps.cue: Stand behind the rope at the edge of the work area with the crew lead.
steps.prompt: Stand behind the rope at the edge of the work area with the crew lead.
steps.title: Stand behind the rope with the crew lead
steps.why: A building site is busy, with tools running and people carrying heavy things. Standing behind the rope keeps the class clear of the crew's work and out of their way. The crew lead watches the site so the class can watch the lesson. Watching from the rope also gives the best view of the whole site at once.

steps.cue: Turn the timer dial to the teacher's setting for both runs.
steps.prompt: Turn the timer dial to the teacher's setting for both runs.
steps.title: Set the drill timer and leave it
steps.why: Both runs must last the same time, or the test is not fair. A longer run would leave more dust on the card whatever else happened. Setting the timer once for both runs keeps the time the same, so only the shroud changes. Scientists call this keeping everything else the same.

steps.cue: Commit when the marker matches the card's colour on the grey scale.

gauge.label: DUST
gauge.missNote: Not matched yet. Slide the marker to the grey that looks like the card.

steps.prompt: Commit when the marker matches the card's colour on the grey scale.
steps.title: Read the dust on the card
steps.why: Matching the card against a grey scale turns what you see into a reading you can compare. A grey card means more dust landed, and a dark clean card means less. Real dust monitors on building sites do the same job much more precisely, and they can measure dust far too fine to see.

steps.cue: Hold the model drill flat against the block until the timer ends.
steps.holdBreakNote: The drill tipped and the shroud lifted. Hold it flat again until the timer ends.
steps.prompt: Hold the model drill flat against the block until the timer ends.
steps.title: Hold the model drill square to the block
steps.why: The shroud only catches dust when it sits flat on the surface. If the drill tips, a gap opens and dust escapes past the shroud. Holding it square is the same skill the real crew uses, and it is what makes the test honest. A steady hand matters more than a fast one here.

steps.cue: Drag the model bench to the side of the work area the breeze blows from.

drag.missNote: That side puts the dust in the breeze's path toward you. Move to where the breeze comes from.

steps.prompt: Drag the model bench to the side of the work area the breeze blows from.
steps.title: Move the bench to where the breeze comes from
steps.why: No dust catcher is perfect, and the breeze carries whatever escapes. Working on the side the breeze comes from sends that little bit of dust away from you instead of into your face. Builders choose where to stand for the same reason. Watching the flag or a strip of tape on a fence shows which way the breeze is blowing.

steps.cue: Look across the site and mark each thing the crew does for clean air.

decoyNotes.sld-cone: It marks the edge of the work, but it does not catch dust.

itemNames.sld-mask: a fitted dust mask on the shelf
itemNames.sld-plan: the dust plan on the board

itemNotes.sld-mask: Worn when the plan asks for it.
itemNotes.sld-plan: It says which tool gets which dust catcher.
itemNotes.sld-vac: No dry sweeping on a dusty floor.

steps.prompt: Look across the site and mark each thing the crew does for clean air.
steps.title: Spot how the crew protects their breathing
steps.why: The national rule for silica dust on building sites asks builders to catch dust at many tools with water or a vacuum, and to clean up without dry sweeping or blowing. When a job still makes dust, the crew's written plan can ask for a fitted mask too. Each of these keeps the air clean where people work, and the plan on the board says which one goes with which tool.

steps.cue: Choose the sentence that says what the two runs showed.
steps.prompt: Choose the sentence that says what the two runs showed.
steps.title: Say what your cards showed
steps.why: Both runs lasted the same time on the same block with clean cards. The card from the run without the shroud came out greyer, and the card from the run with the shroud stayed darker. A good answer says the shroud caught much of the dust, and it does not claim more than the two cards showed.

steps.cue: Keep the marker on the dust puff as the breeze carries it across the site.
steps.holdBreakNote: The marker lost the puff. Find it again and follow it with the breeze.
steps.prompt: Keep the marker on the dust puff as the breeze carries it across the site.
steps.title: Follow the dust puff on the breeze
steps.why: Dust does not stay where it is made. A breeze carries it across the site to people who are not even drilling. Following the puff shows why one crew's dust is everyone's business, and why builders catch it at the drill instead of hoping it blows away.

steps.cue: Write the ways the crew keeps dust out of the air, and name where you learned them.
steps.prompt: Write the ways the crew keeps dust out of the air, and name where you learned them.
steps.title: Record the crew's dust plan in your own words
steps.why: Writing the plan in your own words shows you understood it, and naming the source shows where it came from. A careful scientist or reporter always says where a fact came from, so someone else can check it. Your record can list the shroud, the water, the vacuum and the place to stand, each in one short line.

steps.cue: Tell another group one way builders stop drilling dust from reaching people.
steps.prompt: Tell another group one way builders stop drilling dust from reaching people.
steps.title: Share one way to keep dust out of the air
steps.why: Workers, neighbours and visitors all share the air around a building site. Sharing ways to catch dust helps the class see that small habits, like using a vacuum instead of a brush, keep the air clean for everyone. Hearing another group's way often reminds you of one you forgot.

steps.cue: How does the crew catch drilling dust? Why does it matter where you stand?
steps.prompt: How does the crew catch drilling dust? Why does it matter where you stand?
steps.title: Check in before leaving the site
steps.why: The crew talks over each visit before the class leaves the site. Each learner names a way to catch dust and says why the breeze matters. If anyone thinks the dust is just dirt, the group sorts it out now. Then everyone leaves knowing the same few habits.
